html:
1What You Will Learn

  • Define the roles and responsibilities of AI governance stakeholders
  • Build cross-functional collaboration into the program
  • Create a training and awareness program for every stakeholder group
  • Differentiate governance approaches by the organization's size, maturity, sector and risk tolerance
  • Tell developers, providers, deployers and users apart by their governance duties

2I.B.1: Set out who is responsible for what in AI governance

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Define, so the depth is Remember. The course has 2 practice questions on this indicator.

Running case

Who Owns What at Helios?

  • Samira Haddad, the Chief AI Officer, must stand up an AI governance committee
  • Lucia Moreno's recruiters will use the hiring tool every day and have never been trained on it
  • Veridex supplies the tool; Helios uses it in its own hiring
  • You must say who decides, who advises, who checks and who is trained

Who Does What in AI Governance

  • Board and executives: set strategy and risk tolerance, provide resources and take responsibility for decisions about AI risk (NIST GOVERN 2.3)
  • AI governance committee and Chief AI Officer: set policy, approve high-risk use cases, track the inventory
  • Legal and privacy: interpret laws, run privacy and impact assessments
  • Security and risk: test and monitor threats, set the risk process
  • HR, product and business owners, data science: train people, own use cases, build and operate systems

Exam tip

Read a role question as a duty question: who decides, who advises, who builds, who checks.

The Three Lines Applied to AI Beyond the BoK

  • Governing body: accountable to stakeholders; ensures structures and processes for effective governance
  • First line: delivers the product or service and manages risk: business owners, product teams, data science
  • Second line: expertise, support, monitoring and challenge: risk, compliance, legal, privacy, security, the AI governance office
  • Third line: internal audit, independent and objective assurance to the governing body
  • First and second line roles can be blended or separated; the third line stays independent

Exam tip

Independent assurance means internal audit, not the committee that wrote the policy.

What Legal, Privacy, Security, Risk and HR Each Bring

Function AI governance duty Helios example
Legal track AI and sector law, review contracts and claims Jonas Weber reviews the Veridex agreement
Privacy lawful basis, notices, data subject rights, impact assessments an EU applicant asks what Helios holds
Security protect models, data and pipelines; test for attacks Mei Tanaka tests the assistant for abuse
Risk and compliance risk process, controls, monitoring of policy tracks risk in the AI inventory
HR training, role changes, fair use in hiring Lucia Moreno's recruiters need training
Business owner owns the use case, its outcomes and its risk Anika Berg answers for the assistant
Exam tip

The business owner of a use case owns its risk; legal, privacy and security advise and check.

Accountability in Writing

  • NIST asks that roles, responsibilities and lines of communication for AI risk be documented and clear to everyone (GOVERN 2.1)
  • Executive leadership takes responsibility for decisions about AI risk in development and deployment (GOVERN 2.3)
  • Document decision rights: who proposes, who approves, who can stop a system
  • Name an escalation path from the team to the committee to the board
  • Define roles for human oversight of each system (GOVERN 3.2)
  • A simple responsibility matrix (who is responsible, accountable, consulted, informed) keeps the roles from blurring
Exam tip

If a question says responsibilities were unclear, the fix is a documented role and escalation path.

3I.B.2: Build cross-functional collaboration into the program

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Establish, so the depth is Apply. The course has 1 practice question on this indicator.

Cross-Functional Collaboration

  • AI risk cuts across law, data, security, people and product, so no single function can govern it
  • A cross-functional committee brings these views to each decision
  • NIST: decision-making is informed by a diverse team (GOVERN 3.1)
  • Make collaboration work: a charter, a regular cadence, a clear intake route for new use cases and an escalation path
  • Give the committee decision rights, not only advice

Exam tip

Collaboration is judged by effect: use cases get reviewed from every angle before approval.

A Range of Expertise and Viewpoints

  • NIST asks for teams diverse in demographics, disciplines, experience, expertise and backgrounds
  • Different disciplines catch different risks: lawyers see liability, engineers see failure modes, HR sees fairness
  • Affected people (candidates, customers, frontline staff) see harms the builders miss
  • Silos hide risk: a model approved by data science alone may never meet legal or privacy review
  • Helios: the committee adds recruiters and support leads, and consults candidate and customer feedback
Exam tip

When a question asks how to improve effectiveness, widen who is in the room, not just how often they meet.

4I.B.3: Run training and awareness on AI for every stakeholder group

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Create, so the depth is Create. The course has 1 practice question on this indicator.

Training and Awareness: Who Needs What

  • Program content: AI terminology, strategy and governance
  • Executives: strategy, risk tolerance, accountability
  • Builders (data science, engineering): governance requirements, documentation, testing and bias
  • Business users and recruiters: how the tool works, its limits, when to escalate
  • Legal and procurement: laws, vendor terms, third-party risk
  • All staff: basics, acceptable use, how to raise a concern

Exam tip

One generic course for everyone is the wrong answer; training is matched to role.

The AI Literacy Duty in the EU AI Act Beyond the BoK [Dates] [Verify live]

  • Article 4 applies to providers and deployers of AI systems, whatever the risk level
  • Applies since 2 February 2025 (Article 113)
  • As now worded, they take measures to support AI literacy of staff and others operating AI for them, considering knowledge, experience, education, training, the context of use and the people affected
  • It does not require guaranteeing a specific literacy level for any individual
  • The Digital Omnibus on AI rewrote the Article; earlier it asked providers and deployers to ensure, to their best extent, a sufficient level
  • As of 27 October 2026: check the consolidated text; the Commission and Member States support organizations, especially small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs)
Exam tip

Whichever wording a question uses, the duty is training matched to the people and the context, for every provider and deployer.

Building a Training Program That Works

  • Assess needs: who uses, builds, buys and oversees AI, and what each knows
  • Design by role: short, practical modules in the language of the audience
  • Deliver and record: keep attendance, as evidence for audit and regulators
  • Check understanding: quizzes and scenarios, not only completion
  • Refresh: when systems, rules or incidents change what people must know (GOVERN 2.2 asks that personnel and partners be trained for their duties)

Exam tip

Training is a cycle, not an event: it is repeated when systems, rules or roles change.

5I.B.4: Fit the governance approach to the organization

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Differentiate, so the depth is Analyze. The course has 1 practice question on this indicator.

Fitting the Approach to the Organization

  • Size: a small firm uses a named owner and light process; a large one a committee and several lines
  • Maturity: early programs start with an inventory and basic policy; mature ones add metrics, audits and automation
  • Industry: regulated sectors add sector rules on top of AI rules
  • Products and services: systems that affect people's rights or safety need stronger controls
  • Objectives and risk tolerance: the willingness to accept risk sets thresholds and the amount of review (GOVERN 1.3)

Exam tip

A comparison question wants a fit: more formal for large, regulated or high-risk, lighter for small and low-risk, never none.

Governance Operating Models

Model How it works Fits Watch for
Centralized one team sets and runs governance for all AI smaller or highly regulated organizations bottleneck, distance from the business
Federated (hub and spoke) a central team sets policy, business units run their own AI within it large, diverse organizations uneven practice across units
Decentralized each unit governs itself very early stage only gaps, inconsistency, hidden risk
  • Helios: a hybrid; a central committee sets policy, and business units run their AI with its approval
Exam tip

Hybrid or hub-and-spoke is the usual answer for a large company with many units.

6I.B.5: Tell developers, providers, deployers and users apart by their governance duties

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Identify, so the depth is Understand. The course has 1 practice question on this indicator.

The Actors in the AI Chain Beyond the BoK

  • Developer: designs, builds and trains the model or system
  • Provider: places the system on the market or puts it into service under its own name (often the developer, sometimes not)
  • Deployer: uses the system under its own authority in its operations
  • User: the person who interacts with the system or its output; may be an employee or a member of the public
  • Importers and distributors sit in the supply chain and carry their own duties

Exam tip

One company can hold several roles for different systems; assign the role per system.

The AI Act's Names for the Roles Beyond the BoK

Term (Article 3) Meaning in short
Provider (3) develops or has developed a system or general-purpose model and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name or trademark
Deployer (4) uses an AI system under its authority, except for personal non-professional use
Authorized representative (5) established in the Union, holds a written mandate from a provider
Importer (6) established in the Union, places on the market a system bearing a third-country person's name or trademark
Distributor (7) in the supply chain, neither provider nor importer, makes a system available on the Union market
Operator (8) the umbrella term: provider, product manufacturer, deployer, authorized representative, importer or distributor
Exam tip

The Act speaks of deployers, not users; a user is an individual, a deployer is an organization acting under its authority.

Responsibilities, Opportunities and Needs by Role

Role Governance responsibility Opportunity Need
Developer document design, test for bias and safety build governance in from the start clear requirements, quality data
Provider meet legal duties, supply instructions and information earn trust with transparent products feedback on use and incidents
Deployer fit the system to the use, oversee it, monitor choose vendors on evidence documentation and support from the provider
User use the system as intended, report problems give frontline feedback training, clear information, a way to complain
  • Helios: Veridex is the provider of the hiring tool; Helios is its deployer; recruiters are users
Exam tip

Deployers depend on providers' information; asking for it in the contract is part of governance.

7Exam Q&A

7.1 Practice questions (one best answer, or select exactly the number the question asks for)

S1Samira Haddad wants independent assurance, reporting to the board, that Helios's AI governance and risk management are adequate and effective. Which function should provide it?

  • AData science, which builds and tunes the models used in hiring
  • BThe AI governance committee, which writes the policies under review
  • CInternal audit, acting as an independent third line
  • DThe privacy team, which advises on the rules for personal data
Show the answer

Answer: C. Independent and objective assurance on governance and risk management is the third line, internal audit, accountable to the governing body. The builders and the committee that wrote the policy cannot independently assure their own work, and the privacy team advises rather than audits.

S2Which responsibility belongs to executive leadership in an AI governance program?

  • ALabeling the training examples for the models that the company builds
  • BOwning the decisions about the risks of developing and deploying AI
  • CRunning the daily performance dashboards for the deployed models
  • DDrafting the technical documentation for each system release before launch
Show the answer

Answer: B. Executive leadership sets risk tolerance and takes responsibility for decisions about AI risk. Data labeling, dashboards and technical documentation are operational tasks for the teams that build and run the systems.

S3A company's AI governance committee has only data scientists and one lawyer, and use cases are approved with little challenge. Which TWO additions would best improve its effectiveness and range of expertise? (Select TWO.)

  • AA second senior data scientist to speed up technical review
  • BA privacy specialist who can assess data and notice issues
  • CThe vendor's account manager, given a voting seat
  • DA business owner who uses the system and sees its effects
  • EA second lawyer to double the legal opinions
Show the answer

Answer: B, D. A privacy specialist and a business owner bring new disciplines and the view of those who use the system. More of the same expertise adds little, and a vendor representative with a vote creates a conflict of interest.

S4A company plans AI training for recruiters, developers, executives and buyers, and must also meet the EU AI literacy duty. Which plan best meets the stakeholders' needs?

  • AOne technical course for the developers, because they are the people who build and tune the systems
  • BA one-time video for new hires, kept on file as evidence that the company trained staff
  • CTraining for the teams that run high-risk systems, since the duty is aimed at those systems
  • DRole-based training on AI terminology, strategy and governance for each group's needs and context
Show the answer

Answer: D. The program is meant for all stakeholders and covers terminology, strategy and governance, matched to what each group knows and how it uses AI. The EU duty reaches providers and deployers regardless of risk level, and a one-off video or developer-only course falls short.

S5A 40-person startup uses a third-party chatbot, and a multinational bank deploys credit-scoring models. How should their governance approaches differ?

  • AThe startup uses light, risk-based controls under a named owner; the bank uses a formal committee and stricter tolerance
  • BBoth use the same committee, the same documentation and the same approval gates, so that practice stays consistent everywhere
  • COnly the bank needs any governance, because a startup using a chatbot is too small to create meaningful AI risk
  • DThe startup needs the framework more than the bank, because small organizations lack the experience to manage AI risk
Show the answer

Answer: A. The approach should fit size, sector, products and risk tolerance: a regulated bank scoring credit needs formality and challenge, while a small firm using a chatbot needs proportionate controls. A uniform approach over-burdens one and under-protects the other, and no organization needs none.

S6Helios uses the Veridex hiring tool under its own authority to screen applicants. Veridex makes the tool available under its own name. Which TWO statements describe the roles correctly? (Select TWO.)

  • AVeridex is the provider of the system
  • BHelios is the provider, because it uses the tool in its business
  • CHelios is the deployer of the system
  • DVeridex is a deployer, because it supports the tool after sale
  • EThe applicants are deployers, because the tool scores them
Show the answer

Answer: A, C. The party that makes the system available under its own name is the provider, and the organization that uses it under its own authority is the deployer. Using a system does not make Helios a provider, supporting it does not make Veridex a deployer, and applicants are people affected by it.

8Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Roles leadership decides risk tolerance, the committee sets policy, functions advise, business owners own use cases, audit assures
Collaboration diverse, cross-functional, with a charter, cadence and decision rights
Training by audience, covering terminology, strategy and governance; a cycle, not an event; Article 4 duty
Approach fits size, maturity, sector, products, objectives and risk tolerance
Actors developer, provider, deployer, user; roles are per system
